# A topological exact-constant center-transversal lemma

This is a continuous auxiliary statement. It does not construct a point of
an arbitrary mixed-integer set. Its proof uses the independently audited
continuous optimal-depth theorem in `candidate 0f025bdf9a51573b`.

## Theorem

Let r>=2. Let mu_1,mu_2 be probability measures on R^r with integrable
log-concave densities of full-dimensional support. There exists an affine
line L such that, for each i=1,2 and every closed halfspace H containing L,

    mu_i(H)>=( (r-1)/r )^(r-1)=gamma_(r-1).          (1)

In particular, if the measures are uniform on convex bodies K_1,K_2,
the line intersects both bodies and simultaneously has the stated
halfspace guarantee for both. The line direction is not prescribed.

The following proof gives existence and all selection/limit details. It
does not assume continuity of deepest points, which can fail for a
nonunique optimum.

## 1. Continuous strict-depth selections in moving hyperplanes

Fix 0<a<gamma_(r-1). For a unit vector u let E(u)=u^perp and let pi_u be
orthogonal projection onto E(u). Define

    F_i(u)={c in E(u): mu_i({x:b dot x>=b dot c})>=a
                     for every unit b in E(u)}.

By the classical Prekopa theorem, the push-forward (pi_u)_#mu_i has a
log-concave density on E(u). Its support has nonempty relative interior,
since the original positive set contains a ball. The continuous
optimal-depth theorem in dimension r-1 supplies a point of depth at
least gamma_(r-1)>a. Thus F_i(u) is nonempty and has nonempty relative
interior. It is convex: for any fixed b, the allowed thresholds b dot c
form an interval. It is closed by continuity of cap probabilities.

The sets F_i(u) are bounded uniformly over u. If c belongs to F_i(u)
and c!=0, choose b=c/|c|. The cap through c is contained in
{x:|x|>=|c|}; since its mass is at least a, tightness of the probability
measure bounds |c| independently of u. Consequently F_i(u) is compact.

Choose c_i(u) to be the point of F_i(u) minimizing |c|^2. Strict
convexity of that objective gives uniqueness. We claim this selection
is continuous in u, as a vector in R^r, and is even.

Evenness follows immediately from E(-u)=E(u). To prove continuity, let
u_j tend to u and choose orthogonal maps T_j tending to the identity
with T_j u=u_j. Such maps are obtained by the small rotation in the
plane spanned by u and u_j, fixing its orthogonal complement. The maps

    (c,b) -> mu_i({x:b dot x>=b dot c})

are jointly continuous when b is a unit vector: their indicators
converge away from a hyperplane of mu_i-measure zero, so dominated
convergence applies. This continuity is uniform on compact parameter
sets.

Any limit of a sequence d_j in F_i(u_j) belongs to F_i(u): use the
test normals T_j b for each b in E(u). We also need inner approximation.
Let d belong to F_i(u), and let d_0 be an interior point of F_i(u).
For 0<eta<1, put d_eta=(1-eta)d+eta d_0. Convexity implies that d_eta
is an interior point of F_i(u). Its depth is strictly larger than a.
Indeed, if one cap through it had mass exactly a, moving d_eta a small
distance in that cap's normal direction would remain in F_i(u) but
strictly reduce the cap's mass. Positive depth excludes the boundary
of the projected convex support. The log-concave projected density
is continuous and positive in that support's relative interior, so
it has a positive lower bound on a small ball about d_eta in E(u).
The corresponding small slab has positive projected measure. This
is a contradiction.

Compactness of the sphere of normals makes the strict depth gap at
d_eta uniform. Joint continuity then gives T_j d_eta in F_i(u_j) for
all sufficiently large j. Uniform boundedness makes any subsequence
of the minimizing c_i(u_j) have a convergent subsequence. Its limit
lies in F_i(u), and the preceding approximation gives, for every d
in F_i(u),

    limsup_j |c_i(u_j)| <= |d_eta|.

Letting eta decrease to zero shows that every subsequential limit is
the unique minimum-norm point of F_i(u). This proves continuity of c_i.

The use of a strict level a<gamma_(r-1) is essential to this selection
argument. No continuity claim about the critical-level maximizing
center set is used.

## 2. An even tangent field has a zero

For completeness, the elementary topological fact needed is:

    If V:S^m -> R^(m+1) is continuous, V(u) dot u=0, and
    V(-u)=V(u), then V vanishes somewhere.

Suppose otherwise and put g(u)=V(u)/|V(u)|. The maps

    h_t(u)=cos(pi t/2)u+sin(pi t/2)g(u), 0<=t<=1,

take values on S^m because u and g(u) are orthogonal. Thus g is
homotopic to the identity and has degree one. But g is even. If m
is even, composing with the antipodal map, whose degree is -1, gives
deg g=-deg g and hence deg g=0. If m is odd, g factors through the
oriented double cover S^m -> RP^m, so its degree is twice an integer.
Both conclusions contradict degree one. This proves the fact. Here
only the standard homotopy invariance and multiplicativity of degree
are used; the argument is a usual form of the Borsuk-Ulam obstruction.

## 3. A common line at every strict level

The vector field

    V(u)=c_1(u)-c_2(u)

is continuous, even, and belongs to E(u). By the preceding fact, some
unit u has c_1(u)=c_2(u)=c. Let L_a=c+R u.

Any halfspace containing this whole line has normal b perpendicular
to u. Its boundary can be shifted to c to give a subset still
containing the line. Membership c in both F_i(u) therefore implies
mu_i(H)>=a for every such halfspace and both i.

## 4. Passage to the exact constant and all closed halfspaces

Let a_k increase to gamma_(r-1), with a_k bounded below by a fixed
positive number. Write the lines just constructed as

    L_k=c_k+R u_k,  |u_k|=1, c_k dot u_k=0.

The uniform tail bound from Section 1 bounds |c_k|. Pass to a
subsequence with u_k ->u and c_k ->c; then c dot u=0. Set L=c+R u.

Fix a unit b perpendicular to u and define

    b_k=pi_(u_k)(b)/|pi_(u_k)(b)|.

These are well-defined for large k and converge to b. The halfspaces
{x:b_k dot x>=b_k dot c_k} contain L_k and have mu_i-mass at least
a_k. Their indicators converge outside the hyperplane
{x:b dot x=b dot c}, which is mu_i-null. Dominated convergence gives

    mu_i({x:b dot x>=b dot c})>=gamma_(r-1).

Every closed halfspace containing L has a perpendicular normal and
contains such a boundary-through-c halfspace. This proves (1) with
the exact constant, including all orientations permitted by containing
the line.

For a uniform compact convex body K_i, positive depth of the projected
point c puts c in pi_u(K_i). Hence L intersects K_i. The two intersection
points need not coincide, and this conclusion does not impose any
arithmetic condition on their coordinates.

## Scope and remaining obstacle for a mixed-integer use

The theorem supplies one affine line, not one point, and controls only
halfspaces containing that entire line. It therefore leaves untouched
the essential halfspaces whose normals have a nonzero component along
the line. Even if the two measures are actual integer fibers, a further
proved mechanism would be needed to control these remaining caps at a
single point in one actual fiber. This theorem by itself does not imply
OC, a lifting statement, or a KKM gluing assertion for integer centers.
